walkthroughs.body_html:
Component 3: Spoken Language Endorsement — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Component 3: Spoken Language Endorsement brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Component 3: Spoken Language Endorsement.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why do text types have predictable features?
options: Conventions develop because they serve communicative purpose — a recipe needs imperatives because it instructs; a news report needs the inverted pyramid because of how readers scan.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
Text types have fixed features just because tradition says so.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.

mcqs.q: Why might a writer choose the passive voice?
options: Passive voice means writing in the past tense.
To foreground the patient rather than the agent, omit the agent when unknown or unimportant, sound formal/scientific, or distance the writer from action.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
The passive voice is always grammatically wrong.

mcqs.q: Why does English vocabulary have so many synonyms?
options: Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
English has many synonyms because Shakespeare invented lots of words.
Layered historical contact — Old English, Old Norse, Norman French and Latin — left English with multiple words from different sources for similar concepts (e.g. ask/question/interrogate).
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
